results.title: Automated and adaptive threshold setting: Enabling technology for autonomy and self-management
results.content: Automated and adaptive threshold setting: Enabling technology for autonomy and self-management for ICAC 2005 - IBM Research Automated and adaptive threshold setting: Enabling technology for autonomy and self-management Threshold violations reported for system components signal undesirable conditions in the system. In complex computer systems, characterized by dynamically changing workload patterns and evolving business goals, the pre-computed performance thresholds on the operational values of performance metrics of individual system components are not available. This paper focuses on a fundamental enabling technology for performance management: automatic computation and adaptation of statistically meaningful performance thresholds for system components. We formally define the problem of adaptive threshold setting with controllable accuracy of the thresholds and propose a novel algorithm for solving it. Given a set of Service Level Objectives (SLOs) of the applications executing in the system, our algorithm continually adapts the per-component performance thresholds to the observed SLO violations. The purpose of this continual threshold adaptation is to control the average amounts of false positive and false negative alarms to improve the efficacy of the threshold-based management. In our experiments we achieved a positive predictive value of 92% and a negative predictive value of 93% for component level performance thresholds. ### Mining logs files for computing system management Wei Peng, Tao Li, et al. ### Dynamic protocol selection in open and heterogeneous systems José Ghislain Quenum, Onn Shehory, et al. ### Quickly finding known software problems via automated symptom matching Mark Brodle, Sheng Ma, et al. results.title: Online Hard Example Mining: A Deep Dive into Training Region-Based Object Detectors | SERP AI
results.content: Online Hard Example Mining (OHEM) emerged to address these issues by selectively focusing training on the most informative cases, pushing the boundaries of detector performance across multiple datasets and architectures. This complexity motivated the development of Online Hard Example Mining (OHEM), a technique that specifically targets these challenging examples for training. At its core, OHEM modifies the standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) process to selectively sample training examples based on their current loss. The implementation consists of two primary RoI networks: a read-only network that performs initial forward passes for all input RoIs, and a selection network that implements OHEM logic specifically for hard example identification. This architecture maintains efficiency by performing most forward computations only once per mini-batch while selectively updating gradients for identified hard examples. By implementing OHEM with a single example per batch (N=1), the system maintained consistent performance while reducing GPU memory usage. The threshold-based mechanism allows the network to dynamically adjust its focus based on example difficulty, ensuring consistent performance improvements across different architectures and datasets. The implementation focuses on selectively backpropagating examples with the highest loss, maintaining a carefully managed ratio of negative to positive examples (typically 3:1) during training. This adaptive loss handling proved particularly beneficial in managing the imbalance between positive and negative examples, a common challenge in object detection training. The reduced need for manual parameter tuning and the automated example selection process make OHEM particularly valuable for handling the increasing complexity and size of modern object detection datasets. Unlike SVM-based methods that require careful parameter tuning and iterative refinement, OHEM streamlines the process by focusing directly on maximizing training efficiency through loss-based example selection. The algorithm eliminates the need for bg\_lo thresholds and maintains a consistent example ratio between positive and negative cases, making it particularly robust in scenarios where small dataset sizes may limit training diversity. By dynamically sampling training examples based on current loss, the technique maintains optimal performance across various architectures and dataset sizes while significantly reducing computational overhead compared to alternative approaches. The algorithm's effectiveness across multiple architectures and datasets has established its position as a valuable tool for object detection training, but several implementation challenges remain.

With constant changes in regulations and new emerging threats, imagine the manpower wasted in threshold tuning alone.
